title: de Finibus Bonorum et Malorum
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi048.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: in quibus hoc primum est in quo admirer, cur in gravissimis rebus non delectet eos sermo patrius, cum idem fabellas Latinas ad verbum e Graecis expressas non inviti legant. quis enim tam inimicus paene nomini Romano est, qui Ennii Medeam aut Antiopam Pacuvii spernat aut reiciat, quod se isdem Euripidis fabulis delectari dicat, Latinas litteras oderit? Synephebos ego, inquit, potius Caecilii aut Andriam Terentii quam utramque Menandri legam? A quibus tantum dissentio, ut, cum Sophocles vel optime scripserit Electram, tamen male conversam Atilii mihi legendam putem, de quo Lucilius:
passages.english: Among these, the first thing that makes me wonder is why, in the weightiest matters, their native language does not please them, when these same people are not unwilling to read Latin plays rendered word for word from Greek ones. For who is so nearly an enemy of the Roman name as to scorn or reject Ennius' Medea or Pacuvius' Antiope, saying that he enjoys those same plays of Euripides but hates Latin literature? "Am I," he says, "to read Caecilius' Synephebi or Terence's Andria rather than both [plays] of Menander?" I disagree with these people so much that, although Sophocles wrote his Electra superbly, I still think I ought to read Atilius' poor translation of it, about whom Lucilius [says]:
passages.notes: The quotation from Lucilius that follows is not included in the passage.

passages.original: sed id neque feci adhuc nec mihi tamen, ne faciam, interdictum puto. locos quidem quosdam, si videbitur, transferam, et maxime ab iis, quos modo nominavi, cum inciderit, ut id apte fieri possit, ut ab Homero Ennius, Afranius a Menandro solet. Nec vero, ut noster Lucilius, recusabo, quo minus omnes mea legant. utinam esset ille Persius, Scipio vero et Rutilius multo etiam magis, quorum ille iudicium reformidans Tarentinis ait se et Consentinis et Siculis scribere.
passages.english: But I have not yet done this, and yet I do not think I am forbidden to do it. I shall indeed translate certain passages, if it seems good, and especially from those whom I have just named, when it happens that this can be done fittingly, as Ennius is accustomed to do from Homer, and Afranius from Menander. Nor indeed shall I refuse, as our Lucilius does, to let everyone read my writings. I wish that Persius were alive, and Scipio and Rutilius much more still; dreading their judgement, he says he writes for the people of Tarentum, Consentia and Sicily.
passages.notes: "utinam esset ille Persius" is elliptical; understood as a wish that such critics as Persius were [still] available as readers. Lucilius' line is alluded to, not quoted.

passages.original: quamquam utriusque cum multa non probo, tum illud in primis, quod, cum in rerum natura duo quaerenda sint, unum, quae materia sit, ex qua quaeque res efficiatur, alterum, quae vis sit, quae quidque efficiat, de materia disseruerunt, vim et causam efficiendi reliquerunt. sed hoc commune vitium, illae Epicuri propriae ruinae: censet enim eadem illa individua et solida corpora ferri deorsum suo pondere ad lineam, hunc naturalem esse omnium corporum motum.
passages.english: And yet, while I disapprove of much in both of them, I disapprove above all of this: although in the study of nature there are two things to be investigated, first, what the matter is from which each thing is produced, and second, what the force is that produces each thing, they discussed matter but left aside the force and cause of production. But this is a fault common to both; the following are Epicurus' own downfalls. He holds that those same indivisible and solid bodies are carried downward by their own weight in a straight line, and that this is the natural motion of all bodies.
passages.notes: 'utriusque' refers to Democritus and Epicurus (cf. context).

passages.original: Quae cum dixissem, magis ut illum provocarem quam ut ipse loquerer, tum Triarius leniter arridens: Tu quidem, inquit, totum Epicurum paene e philosophorum choro sustulisti. quid ei reliquisti, nisi te, quoquo modo loqueretur, intellegere, quid diceret? aliena dixit in physicis nec ea ipsa, quae tibi probarentur; si qua in iis corrigere voluit, deteriora fecit.
passages.english: When I had said this, more to provoke him than to do the talking myself, Triarius, smiling gently, said: "You have pretty well removed Epicurus altogether from the chorus of philosophers. What have you left him, except that, however he expressed himself, you understand what he meant? In physics he said things borrowed from others, and not even such as you would approve; where he wanted to correct anything in them, he made it worse."

passages.original: Primum igitur, inquit, sic agam, ut ipsi auctori huius disciplinae placet: constituam, quid et quale sit id, de quo quaerimus, non quo ignorare vos arbitrer, sed ut ratione et via procedat oratio. quaerimus igitur, quid sit extremum et ultimum bonorum, quod omnium philosophorum sententia tale debet esse, ut ad id omnia referri oporteat, ipsum autem nusquam. hoc Epicurus in voluptate ponit, quod summum bonum esse vult, summumque malum dolorem, idque instituit docere sic:
passages.english: "First, then," he said, "I shall proceed as the founder of this school himself prefers: I shall establish what the thing we are investigating is and what kind of thing it is, not because I think you are ignorant of it, but so that the discussion may advance by method and in order. We are asking, then, what is the final and ultimate good, which in the opinion of all philosophers must be such that everything ought to be referred to it, while it itself is referred to nothing. Epicurus places this in pleasure, which he holds to be the highest good, and the greatest evil in pain; and he sets out to teach it as follows:

passages.original: illud enim ipsum, quod quibusdam medium videretur, cum omni dolore careret, non modo voluptatem esse, verum etiam summam voluptatem. quisquis enim sentit, quem ad modum sit affectus, eum necesse est aut in voluptate esse aut in dolore. omnis autem privatione doloris putat Epicurus terminari summam voluptatem, ut postea variari voluptas distinguique possit, augeri amplificarique non possit.
passages.english: [he held that] the very state which seemed to some to be intermediate, when one is free of all pain, is not only pleasure but even the highest pleasure. For whoever is aware of how he is affected must necessarily be either in pleasure or in pain. Moreover, Epicurus thinks that the highest pleasure is bounded by the removal of all pain, so that afterwards pleasure can be varied and diversified, but cannot be increased or enlarged.

passages.original: nam si ea sola voluptas esset, quae quasi titillaret sensus, ut ita dicam, et ad eos cum suavitate afflueret et illaberetur, nec manus esse contenta posset nec ulla pars vacuitate doloris sine iucundo motu voluptatis. sin autem summa voluptas est, ut Epicuro placet, nihil dolere, primum tibi recte, Chrysippe, concessum est nihil desiderare manum, cum ita esset affecta, secundum non recte, si voluptas esset bonum, fuisse desideraturam. idcirco enim non desideraret, quia, quod dolore caret, id in voluptate est.
passages.english: For if pleasure were only that which, so to speak, tickles the senses and flows into them and steals into them with sweetness, neither a hand nor any other part could be content with freedom from pain without a pleasant motion of pleasure. But if the highest pleasure is, as Epicurus holds, to feel no pain, then, Chrysippus, the first point was rightly granted you, that the hand, when so affected, lacked nothing; the second not rightly, that it would have lacked something if pleasure were a good. For the reason it would lack nothing is precisely that whatever is free of pain is in a state of pleasure.

passages.original: cum enim certe nihil homini possit melius esse quam vacare omni dolore et molestia perfruique maximis et animi et corporis voluptatibus, videtisne quam nihil praetermittatur quod vitam adiuvet, quo facilius id, quod propositum est, summum bonum consequamur? clamat Epicurus, is quem vos nimis voluptatibus esse deditum dicitis, non posse iucunde vivi, nisi sapienter, honeste iusteque vivatur, nec sapienter, honeste, iuste, nisi iucunde.
passages.english: For since surely nothing can be better for a human being than to be free of all pain and trouble and to enjoy the greatest pleasures of both mind and body, do you see how nothing is left out that assists life, so that we may more easily attain that which is set before us, the highest good? Epicurus, the man you say is too much given over to pleasures, proclaims that one cannot live pleasantly unless one lives wisely, honourably and justly, nor wisely, honourably and justly unless pleasantly.

passages.original: optime vero Epicurus, quod exiguam dixit fortunam intervenire sapienti maximasque ab eo et gravissimas res consilio ipsius et ratione administrari neque maiorem voluptatem ex infinito tempore aetatis percipi posse, quam ex hoc percipiatur, quod videamus esse finitum.
passages.english: And Epicurus spoke excellently in saying that fortune plays a small part in the life of the wise man, and that his greatest and weightiest affairs are managed by his own judgment and reason, and that no greater pleasure can be obtained from an infinite span of life than is obtained from this one, which we see to be finite.

passages.original: nisi autem rerum natura perspecta erit, nullo modo poterimus sensuum iudicia defendere. quicquid porro animo cernimus, id omne oritur a sensibus; qui si omnes veri erunt, ut Epicuri ratio docet, tum denique poterit aliquid cognosci et percipi. quos qui tollunt et nihil posse percipi dicunt, ii remotis sensibus ne id ipsum quidem expedire possunt, quod disserunt. praeterea sublata cognitione et scientia tollitur omnis ratio et vitae degendae et rerum gerendarum.
passages.english: But unless the nature of things has been thoroughly understood, we shall in no way be able to defend the judgments of the senses. Further, whatever we discern with the mind arises wholly from the senses; and if they are all true, as Epicurus' system teaches, then and only then can anything be known and grasped. Those who do away with them and say that nothing can be grasped cannot, once the senses are removed, even set out the very thing they are arguing. Moreover, when knowledge and understanding are removed, every rational basis both for living one's life and for conducting affairs is removed.

passages.original: Restat locus huic disputationi vel maxime necessarius de amicitia, quam, si voluptas summum sit bonum, affirmatis nullam omnino fore. de qua Epicurus quidem ita dicit, omnium rerum, quas ad beate vivendum sapientia comparaverit, nihil esse maius amicitia, nihil uberius, nihil iucundius. nec vero hoc oratione solum, sed multo magis vita et factis et moribus comprobavit.
passages.english: There remains a topic especially necessary to this discussion, that of friendship, which you maintain will not exist at all if pleasure is the highest good. Concerning it Epicurus says this: of all the things that wisdom has provided for living happily, nothing is greater than friendship, nothing richer, nothing more delightful. And he proved this not only in words, but far more by his life, his deeds and his character.

passages.original: quocirca eodem modo sapiens erit affectus erga amicum, quo in se ipsum, quosque labores propter suam voluptatem susciperet, eosdem suscipiet propter amici voluptatem. quaeque de virtutibus dicta sunt, quem ad modum eae semper voluptatibus inhaererent, eadem de amicitia dicenda sunt. praeclare enim Epicurus his paene verbis: Eadem, inquit, scientia confirmavit animum, ne quod aut sempiternum aut diuturnum timeret malum, quae perspexit in hoc ipso vitae spatio amicitiae praesidium esse firmissimum.
passages.english: Therefore the wise man will be disposed toward his friend just as toward himself, and whatever labours he would undertake for his own pleasure, he will undertake the same for his friend's pleasure. And what has been said about the virtues, how they are always bound up with pleasures, must be said likewise about friendship. For Epicurus put it excellently in nearly these words: "The same knowledge," he says, "that has strengthened the mind not to fear any evil that is everlasting or long-lasting has perceived that in this very span of life the protection of friendship is the most secure."

passages.original: an ille tempus aut in poëtis evolvendis, ut ego et Triarius te hortatore facimus, consumeret, in quibus nulla solida utilitas omnisque puerilis est delectatio, aut se, ut Plato, in musicis, geometria, numeris, astris contereret, quae et a falsis initiis profecta vera esse non possunt et, si essent vera, nihil afferrent, quo iucundius, id est quo melius viveremus, eas ergo artes persequeretur, vivendi artem tantam tamque et operosam et perinde fructuosam relinqueret?
passages.english: Or should he have spent his time either in unrolling the poets, as Triarius and I do at your urging, in whom there is no solid usefulness and all the delight is childish, or, like Plato, worn himself out in music, geometry, numbers and the stars, which, starting from false first principles, cannot be true, and, if they were true, would contribute nothing to make us live more pleasantly, that is, better; should he, then, have pursued those arts, and abandoned the art of living, so great, so laborious and correspondingly so fruitful?

passages.original: sed et illum, quem nominavi, et ceteros sophistas, ut e Platone intellegi potest, lusos videmus a Socrate. is enim percontando atque interrogando elicere solebat eorum opiniones, quibuscum disserebat, ut ad ea, quae ii respondissent, si quid videretur, diceret.
passages.english: But we see that both the man I named and the other sophists were made fun of by Socrates, as can be understood from Plato. For by questioning and interrogating he used to draw out the opinions of those with whom he was conversing, so that he might say what he thought in reply to their answers.
passages.notes: 'The man I named' refers to someone mentioned before this passage (probably Hippias or Gorgias), not identifiable from the text given.

passages.original: Quid ergo? istam voluptatem, inquit, Epicurus ignorat?
passages.english: "What then?" he said. "Is Epicurus unaware of that pleasure?"

passages.original: Tenesne igitur, inquam, Hieronymus Rhodius quid dicat esse summum bonum, quo putet omnia referri oportere?
passages.english: "Do you know, then," I said, "what Hieronymus of Rhodes says is the highest good, to which he thinks everything ought to be referred?"

passages.original: quid enim necesse est, tamquam meretricem in matronarum coetum, sic voluptatem in virtutum concilium adducere? invidiosum nomen est, infame, suspectum. itaque hoc frequenter dici solet a vobis, non intellegere nos, quam dicat Epicurus voluptatem. quod quidem mihi si quando dictum est—est autem dictum non parum saepe—, etsi satis clemens sum in disputando, tamen interdum soleo subirasci. egone non intellego, quid sit ἡδονή Graece, Latine voluptas?
passages.english: For why is it necessary to bring pleasure into the council of the virtues, like a prostitute into a gathering of married women? It is a name that arouses ill will, disreputable, suspect. And so you people often say that we do not understand what pleasure Epicurus means. Whenever this is said to me, and it has been said quite often enough, although I am fairly mild in argument, I nevertheless sometimes get a little angry. Do I not understand what hēdonē is in Greek, voluptas in Latin?

passages.original: ergo illi intellegunt quid Epicurus dicat, ego non intellego? ut scias me intellegere, primum idem esse dico voluptatem, quod ille ἡδονήν. et quidem saepe quaerimus verbum Latinum par Graeco et quod idem valeat; hic nihil fuit, quod quaereremus.
passages.english: So they understand what Epicurus means, and I do not? So that you may know that I understand, first I say that voluptas is the same as what he calls hēdonē. And indeed we often look for a Latin word equal to a Greek one and having the same force; here there was nothing for us to look for.

passages.original: et tamen vide, ne, si ego non intellegam quid Epicurus loquatur, cum Graece, ut videor, luculenter sciam, sit aliqua culpa eius, qui ita loquatur, ut non intellegatur. quod duobus modis sine reprehensione fit, si aut de industria facias, ut Heraclitus, cognomento qui σκοτεινός perhibetur, quia de natura nimis obscure memoravit, aut cum rerum obscuritas, non verborum, facit ut non intellegatur oratio, qualis est in Timaeo Platonis. Epicurus autem, ut opinor, nec non vult, si possit, plane et aperte loqui, nec de re obscura, ut physici, aut artificiosa, ut mathematici, sed de illustri et facili et iam in vulgus pervagata loquitur.
passages.english: And yet consider whether, if I do not understand what Epicurus is saying, though I know Greek, as I think, thoroughly, the fault may not lie in some measure with the man who speaks in such a way as not to be understood. This happens without blame in two ways: either if you do it deliberately, like Heraclitus, who is called by the surname skoteinos [the obscure] because he wrote about nature too obscurely; or when obscurity of the subject matter, not of the words, makes the discourse unintelligible, as is the case in Plato's Timaeus. But Epicurus, in my opinion, is both not unwilling, if he can, to speak plainly and openly, and is speaking not about an obscure subject, like the natural philosophers, nor a technical one, like the mathematicians, but about one that is clear and easy and already widespread among the common people.

passages.original: si enim idem dicit, quod Hieronymus, qui censet summum bonum esse sine ulla molestia vivere, cur mavult dicere voluptatem quam vacuitatem doloris, ut ille facit, qui quid dicat intellegit? sin autem voluptatem putat adiungendam eam, quae sit in motu—sic enim appellat hanc dulcem: in motu, illam nihil dolentis in stabilitate—, quid tendit?
passages.english: For if he means the same as Hieronymus, who holds that the highest good is to live without any trouble, why does he prefer to say 'pleasure' rather than 'freedom from pain', as the latter does, who understands what he is saying? But if he thinks that pleasure in motion must be added—for so he names this sweet kind, 'in motion', and the other, that of one feeling no pain, 'in a stable state'—what is he aiming at?

passages.original: multi enim et magni philosophi haec ultima bonorum iuncta fecerunt, ut Aristoteles virtutis usum cum vitae perfectae prosperitate coniunxit, Callipho adiunxit ad honestatem voluptatem, Diodorus ad eandem honestatem addidit vacuitatem doloris. idem fecisset Epicurus, si sententiam hanc, quae nunc Hieronymi est, coniunxisset cum Aristippi vetere sententia. illi enim inter se dissentiunt. propterea singulis finibus utuntur et, cum uterque Graece egregie loquatur, nec Aristippus, qui voluptatem summum bonum dicit, in voluptate ponit non dolere, neque Hieronymus, qui summum bonum statuit non dolere, voluptatis nomine umquam utitur pro illa indolentia, quippe qui ne in expetendis quidem rebus numeret voluptatem.
passages.english: For many great philosophers have made these ultimate goods combined: thus Aristotle joined the exercise of virtue with prosperity throughout a complete life; Callipho added pleasure to moral goodness; Diodorus added freedom from pain to that same moral goodness. Epicurus would have done the same if he had joined this view, which now belongs to Hieronymus, with the old view of Aristippus. For those two disagree with each other. Therefore they each use a single end, and, since both speak Greek excellently, neither does Aristippus, who calls pleasure the highest good, count absence of pain as pleasure, nor does Hieronymus, who lays down absence of pain as the highest good, ever use the name of pleasure for that painlessness; indeed he does not even number pleasure among things to be sought.

passages.original: Hoc loco tenere se Triarius non potuit. Obsecro, inquit, Torquate, haec dicit Epicurus? quod mihi quidem visus est, cum sciret, velle tamen confitentem audire Torquatum.
passages.english: At this point Triarius could not contain himself. "I beg you, Torquatus," he said, "does Epicurus say these things?" It seemed to me that, though he knew, he nevertheless wanted to hear Torquatus admit it.

passages.original: nemo nostrum istius generis asotos iucunde putat vivere. mundos, elegantis, optimis cocis, pistoribus, piscatu, aucupio, venatione, his omnibus exquisitis, vitantes cruditatem, quibus vinum defusum e pleno sit chrysizon, ut ait Lucilius, cui nihildum situlus et sacculus abstulerit, adhibentis ludos et quae sequuntur, illa, quibus detractis clamat Epicurus se nescire quid sit bonum; adsint etiam formosi pueri, qui ministrent, respondeat his vestis, argentum, Corinthium, locus ipse, aedificium—hos ergo asotos bene quidem vivere aut beate numquam dixerim.
passages.english: None of us thinks that profligates of that kind live pleasantly. But [take] refined, elegant men, with the best cooks and bakers, with fish, fowl and game, all of these choice, avoiding indigestion; men who have wine poured off from a full jar, "golden-hued," as Lucilius says, "from which the strainer and bag have not yet taken anything"; men who bring in entertainments and what follows them, those things without which Epicurus cries that he does not know what the good is; let there also be handsome boys to wait on them, and let the clothing, silver, Corinthian bronze, the place itself and the building match these—these profligates, then, I would never say live well or happily.
passages.notes: "chrysizon" is a Greek word (golden-coloured) quoted from Lucilius; "situlus" is an uncertain reading, perhaps for a strainer or sieve (some editions read "sacculus" alone or "saccus").

passages.original: quid bene? dicet Lucilius: cocto, condito, sed cedo caput cenae: sermone bono, quid ex eo? si quaeris, libenter; veniebat enim ad cenam, ut animo quieto satiaret desideria naturae. recte ergo is negat umquam bene cenasse Gallonium, recte miserum, cum praesertim in eo omne studium consumeret.
passages.english: What [is it to dine] well? Lucilius will say: "[On food] cooked and seasoned, but give me the main course of the dinner: good conversation." What follows from that? If you ask, [he dined] with pleasure; for he came to dinner in order to satisfy the desires of nature with a calm mind. Rightly, then, he denies that Gallonius ever dined well, rightly [calls him] wretched, especially since he spent all his effort on this.
passages.notes: The subject "he" is Laelius, as the following context shows; the Lucilius quotation is fragmentary and its punctuation uncertain.

passages.original: hi non viderunt, ut ad cursum equum, ad arandum bovem, ad indagandum canem, sic hominem ad duas res, ut ait Aristoteles, ad intellegendum et agendum, esse natum quasi mortalem deum, contraque ut tardam aliquam et languidam pecudem ad pastum et ad procreandi voluptatem hoc divinum animal ortum esse voluerunt, quo nihil mihi videtur absurdius.
passages.english: These men did not see that, just as the horse is born for running, the ox for ploughing, the dog for tracking, so man, as Aristotle says, is born for two things, for understanding and for acting, as a kind of mortal god; on the contrary, they would have it that this divine creature came into being, like some slow and sluggish beast, for feeding and for the pleasure of procreation, and nothing seems to me more absurd than this.

passages.original: Nec vero audiendus Hieronymus, cui summum bonum est idem, quod vos interdum vel potius nimium saepe dicitis, nihil dolere. non enim, si malum est dolor, carere eo malo satis est ad bene vivendum. hoc dixerit potius Ennius: Nimium boni est, cui nihil est mali. nos beatam vitam non depulsione mali, sed adeptione boni iudicemus, nec eam cessando, sive gaudentem, ut Aristippus, sive non dolentem, ut hic, sed agendo aliquid considerandove quaeramus.
passages.english: Nor indeed should we listen to Hieronymus, for whom the highest good is the same thing you sometimes, or rather far too often, speak of: to feel no pain. For if pain is an evil, to be free of that evil is not enough for living well. Ennius might rather say this: "He has more than enough good who has no evil." Let us judge the happy life not by the warding off of evil but by the gaining of good, and let us seek it not by inactivity, whether rejoicing, as Aristippus [would have it], or free from pain, as this man [would], but by doing or contemplating something.

passages.original: eademque ratio fecit hominem hominum adpetentem cumque iis natura et sermone et usu congruentem, ut profectus a caritate domesticorum ac suorum serpat longius et se implicet primum civium, deinde omnium mortalium societate atque, ut ad Archytam scripsit Plato, non sibi se soli natum meminerit, sed patriae, sed suis, ut perexigua pars ipsi relinquatur.
passages.english: And the same reason has made man desirous of [the company of] men, and in accord with them by nature, by speech and by practice, so that, setting out from affection for his household and his own people, he may spread further and bind himself first in the fellowship of his fellow citizens, then of all mortals, and, as Plato wrote to Archytas, may remember that he was born not for himself alone but for his country and for his own people, so that only a very small part is left to himself.

passages.original: Habes undique expletam et perfectam, Torquate, formam honestatis, quae tota quattuor his virtutibus, quae a te quoque commemoratae sunt, continetur. hanc se tuus Epicurus omnino ignorare dicit quam aut qualem esse velint qui honestate summum bonum metiantur. Si enim ad honestatem omnia referant neque in ea voluptatem dicant inesse, ait eos voce inani sonare— his enim ipsis verbis utitur—neque intellegere nec videre sub hanc vocem honestatis quae sit subicienda sententia.
passages.english: You have, Torquatus, the form of the honourable filled out and completed on every side, and it is wholly contained in these four virtues, which you too have mentioned. Your Epicurus says that he is entirely ignorant of what this is, or of what sort those who measure the highest good by the honourable would have it be. For if they refer everything to the honourable and say that pleasure has no place in it, he says that they are making an empty noise with their voices (these are the very words he uses), and that they do not understand or see what meaning is to be placed under this word 'honourable'.

passages.original: Decius, princeps in ea familia consulatus, cum se devoverat et equo admisso in mediam aciem Latinorum irruebat, aliquid de voluptatibus suis cogitabat? ubi ut eam caperet aut quando? cum sciret confestim esse moriendum eamque mortem ardentiore studio peteret, quam Epicurus voluptatem petendam putat. quod quidem eius factum nisi esset iure laudatum, non esset imitatus quarto consulatu suo filius, neque porro ex eo natus cum Pyrrho bellum gerens consul cecidisset in proelio seque e continenti genere tertiam victimam rei publicae praebuisset.
passages.english: Decius, the first in that family to hold the consulship, when he had devoted himself and, giving his horse its head, was charging into the middle of the Latin battle line, was he thinking anything about his own pleasures? Where was he to take it, or when? For he knew that he must die at once, and he sought that death with more ardent zeal than Epicurus thinks pleasure should be sought. And indeed, had this deed of his not been rightly praised, his son would not have imitated it in his fourth consulship, nor again would the son born of him, when as consul he was waging war with Pyrrhus, have fallen in battle and offered himself as the third victim from an unbroken line to the commonwealth.

passages.original: qui enim existimabit posse se miserum esse beatus non erit. nam cum suscepta semel est beata vita, tam permanet quam ipsa illa effectrix beatae vitae sapientia neque expectat ultimum tempus aetatis, quod Croeso scribit Herodotus praeceptum a Solone. At enim, quem ad modum tute dicebas, negat Epicurus diuturnitatem quidem temporis ad beate vivendum aliquid afferre, nec minorem voluptatem percipi in brevitate temporis, quam si illa sit sempiterna.
passages.english: For whoever thinks he can be wretched will not be happy. For once a happy life has been taken up, it lasts as long as wisdom itself, the producer of the happy life, and it does not wait for the last period of one's lifetime, as Herodotus writes Solon advised Croesus. But, as you yourself were saying, Epicurus denies that length of time adds anything to living happily, and [says] that no less pleasure is felt in a brief space of time than if it were everlasting.

passages.original: non enim in ipsa sapientia positum est beatum esse, sed in iis rebus, quas sapientia comparat ad voluptatem. totum autem id externum est, et quod externum, id in casu est. ita fit beatae vitae domina fortuna, quam Epicurus ait exiguam intervenire sapienti.
passages.english: For being happy is not located in wisdom itself, but in those things which wisdom procures for the sake of pleasure. But all that is external, and what is external lies in chance. So fortune becomes mistress of the happy life, fortune which Epicurus says plays only a slight part for the wise man.

passages.original: Age, inquies, ista parva sunt. Sapientem locupletat ipsa natura, cuius divitias Epicurus parabiles esse docuit. Haec bene dicuntur, nec ego repugno, sed inter sese ipsa pugnant. negat enim tenuissimo victu, id est contemptissimis escis et potionibus, minorem voluptatem percipi quam rebus exquisitissimis ad epulandum.
passages.english: "Come," you will say, "those are small matters. Nature herself makes the wise man rich, and Epicurus taught that her riches are easily obtained." This is well said, and I do not oppose it, but these things are at war with one another. For he denies that less pleasure is gained from the plainest fare, that is, from the most despised foods and drinks, than from the most exquisite things for feasting.

passages.original: Verum esto; consequatur summas voluptates non modo parvo, sed per me nihilo, si potest; sit voluptas non minor in nasturcio illo, quo vesci Persas esse solitos scribit Xenophon, quam in Syracusanis mensis, quae a Platone graviter vituperantur; sit, inquam, tam facilis, quam vultis, comparatio voluptatis, quid de dolore dicemus? cuius tanta tormenta sunt, ut in iis beata vita, si modo dolor summum malum est, esse non possit. ipse enim Metrodorus, paene alter Epicurus, beatum esse describit his fere verbis: cum corpus bene constitutum sit et sit exploratum ita futurum. an id exploratum cuiquam potest esse, quo modo se hoc habiturum sit corpus, non dico ad annum, sed ad vesperum? dolor ergo, id est summum malum, metuetur semper, etiamsi non aderit;
passages.english: But let it be so; let him obtain the highest pleasures not only for little but, for all I care, for nothing, if he can; let there be no less pleasure in that cress which Xenophon writes the Persians used to eat than in the Syracusan tables which Plato severely censures; let the procuring of pleasure be, I say, as easy as you like: what shall we say about pain? Its tortures are so great that amid them a happy life cannot exist, at least if pain is the highest evil. For Metrodorus himself, almost a second Epicurus, describes being happy in roughly these words: when the body is in good condition and it is assured that it will be so in future. But can anyone be assured of how his body will be, I do not say a year from now, but by evening? Pain, then, that is, the highest evil, will always be feared, even when it is not present;

passages.original: Traditur, inquit, ab Epicuro ratio neglegendi doloris. Iam id ipsum absurdum, maximum malum neglegi. sed quae tandem ista ratio est? Maximus dolor, inquit, brevis est. Primum quid tu dicis breve? deinde dolorem quem maximum?
passages.english: "Epicurus," he says, "hands down a method for disregarding pain." Already that very thing is absurd, that the greatest evil should be disregarded. But what, pray, is this method? "The greatest pain," he says, "is brief." First, what do you call brief? Next, what pain do you call greatest?

passages.original: Sic Epicurus: Philocteta, st! brevis dolor. At iam decimum annum in spelunca iacet. Si longus, levis; dat enim intervalla et relaxat.
passages.english: So says Epicurus: "Philoctetes, hush! The pain is brief." But he has now been lying in the cave for the tenth year. "If long, it is light; for it gives intervals and eases off."
passages.notes: 'st!' is an interjection calling for silence.

passages.original: Audi, ne longe abeam, moriens quid dicat Epicurus, ut intellegas facta eius cum dictis discrepare: Epicurus Hermarcho salutem. Cum ageremus, inquit, vitae beatum et eundem supremum diem, scribebamus haec. tanti autem aderant vesicae et torminum morbi, ut nihil ad eorum magnitudinem posset accedere.
passages.english: Hear, so as not to go far afield, what Epicurus says when dying, so that you may understand that his deeds are at odds with his words: "Epicurus to Hermarchus, greetings. While we were spending," he says, "the happy and at the same time the last day of my life, we were writing this. Such great afflictions of the bladder and bowels were upon me that nothing could be added to their severity."

passages.original: ipse etiam dicit Epicurus ne argumentandum quidem esse de voluptate, quod sit positum iudicium eius in sensibus, ut commoneri nos satis sit, nihil attineat doceri. quare illa nobis simplex fuit in utramque partem disputatio.
passages.english: Epicurus himself even says that there is no need even to argue about pleasure, because the judgement of it is located in the senses, so that it is enough for us to be reminded, and there is no point in being taught. So that debate, on both sides, was a simple one for us.

passages.original: Totum genus hoc Zeno et qui ab eo sunt aut non potuerunt tueri aut noluerunt, certe reliquerunt. quamquam scripsit artem rhetoricam Cleanthes, Chrysippus etiam, sed sic, ut, si quis obmutescere concupierit, nihil aliud legere debeat. itaque vides, quo modo loquantur. nova verba fingunt, deserunt usitata.
passages.english: This whole kind [of discourse] Zeno and his followers either could not maintain or would not; at any rate they abandoned it. Cleanthes did write a handbook of rhetoric, and so did Chrysippus, but in such a way that, if anyone wanted to be struck dumb, he should read nothing else. And so you see how they speak. They invent new words and abandon the customary ones.

passages.original: sequuntur enim ea, quae tu scientissime complexus es, omnium insipientiam, iniustitiam, alia vitia similia esse, omniaque peccata esse paria, eosque, qui natura doctrinaque longe ad virtutem processissent, nisi eam plane consecuti essent, summe esse miseros, neque inter eorum vitam et improbissimorum quicquam omnino interesse, ut Plato, tantus ille vir, si sapiens non fuerit, nihilo melius quam quivis improbissimus nec beatius vixerit. haec videlicet est correctio philosophiae veteris et emendatio, quae omnino aditum habere nullum potest in urbem, in forum, in curiam.
passages.english: For there follow those doctrines which you summarized most expertly: that the folly, the injustice and the other vices of all men are alike, and that all wrongdoings are equal; and that those who by nature and training had advanced far toward virtue, unless they had fully attained it, are supremely wretched, and that there is no difference at all between their life and that of the most wicked, so that Plato, that great man, if he was not a wise man, lived no better and no more happily than any most wicked person you like. This, evidently, is the correction and improvement of the old philosophy, which can have no access whatever to the city, the forum, or the senate-house.

passages.original: cuiuscumque enim modi animal constitueris, necesse est, etiamsi id sine corpore sit, ut fingimus, tamen esse in animo quaedam similia eorum, quae sunt in corpore, ut nullo modo, nisi ut exposui, constitui possit finis bonorum. Chrysippus autem exponens differentias animantium ait alias earum corpore excellere, alias autem animo, non nullas valere utraque re; deinde disputat, quod cuiusque generis animantium statui deceat extremum. cum autem hominem in eo genere posuisset, ut ei tribueret animi excellentiam, summum bonum id constituit, non ut excellere animus, sed ut nihil esse praeter animum videretur. uno autem modo in virtute sola summum bonum recte poneretur, si quod esset animal, quod totum ex mente constaret, id ipsum tamen sic, ut ea mens nihil haberet in se, quod esset secundum naturam, ut valitudo est.
passages.english: For whatever kind of living creature you construct, it is necessary, even if it is without a body, as we imagine, that there nevertheless be in its mind certain things similar to those that are in the body, so that the end of goods can in no way be established except as I have set out. Chrysippus, however, setting out the differences among living creatures, says that some of them excel in body, others in mind, and some are strong in both; then he discusses what ultimate end ought to be established for each kind of creature. But when he had placed man in that kind to which he attributed excellence of mind, he established the supreme good in such a way that it seemed not that the mind excelled, but that there was nothing besides the mind. The supreme good would rightly be placed in virtue alone in one way only: if there were some creature consisting wholly of mind, and that too in such a way that this mind had nothing in itself that was in accordance with nature, as health is.

passages.original: Sin dicit obscurari quaedam nec apparere, quia valde parva sint, nos quoque concedimus; quod dicit Epicurus etiam de voluptate, quae minimae sint voluptates, eas obscurari saepe et obrui. sed non sunt in eo genere tantae commoditates corporis tamque productae temporibus tamque multae. itaque in quibus propter eorum exiguitatem obscuratio consequitur, saepe accidit, ut nihil interesse nostra fateamur, sint illa necne sint, ut in sole, quod a te dicebatur, lucernam adhibere nihil interest aut teruncium adicere Croesi pecuniae.
passages.english: But if he says that certain things are obscured and do not show, because they are very small, we too grant it; Epicurus says this even of pleasure, that the smallest pleasures are often obscured and overwhelmed. But in that class are not advantages of the body so great, so prolonged in time, and so numerous. And so, in the cases where obscuring follows because of their smallness, it often happens that we admit it makes no difference to us whether they exist or not, just as in sunlight, as you were saying, it makes no difference to bring in a lamp, or to add a quarter-as to the wealth of Croesus.
passages.notes: teruncium: a tiny coin, a quarter of an as.

passages.original: hoc vero te ferre non potuisse, quod antiqui illi quasi barbati, ut nos de nostris solemus dicere, crediderint, eius, qui honeste viveret, si idem etiam bene valeret, bene audiret, copiosus esset, optabiliorem fore vitam melioremque et magis expetendam quam illius, qui aeque vir bonus multis modis esset, ut Ennii Alcmaeo, círcumventus mórbo, exilio atque ínopia.
passages.english: But [you said] you could not bear this: that those ancients, bearded as it were, as we are accustomed to say of our own [forebears], believed that the life of one who lived honourably, if he also had good health, a good reputation and plenty of wealth, would be more desirable, better and more worth seeking than that of one who, an equally good man, was in many ways, like Ennius' Alcmaeon, "beset by disease, exile and want."

passages.original: cum enim, quod honestum sit, id solum bonum esse confirmatur, tollitur cura valitudinis, diligentia rei familiaris, administratio rei publicae, ordo gerendorum negotiorum, officia vitae, ipsum denique illud honestum, in quo uno vultis esse omnia, deserendum est. quae diligentissime contra Aristonem dicuntur a Chrysippo. ex ea difficultate illae fallaciloquae, ut ait Accius,malitiae natae sunt.
passages.english: For when it is maintained that what is honourable is the only good, care of health, management of one's household, administration of the state, the conduct of affairs, the duties of life are all done away with, and finally that very honourable itself, in which alone you say everything lies, must be abandoned. These points are argued most carefully by Chrysippus against Aristo. From that difficulty arose those "deceit-speaking tricks," as Accius says.

passages.original: illa autem, morbum, egestatem, dolorem, non appello mala, sed, si libet,reiectanea. itaque illa non dico me expetere, sed legere, nec optare, sed sumere, contraria autem non fugere, sed quasi secernere. Quid ait Aristoteles reliquique Platonis alumni? Se omnia, quae secundum naturam sint, bona appellare, quae autem contra, mala.
passages.english: But those things, disease, poverty, pain, I do not call evils, but, if you like, 'rejectables'. And so I do not say that I seek the former, but that I select them, nor that I wish for them, but that I take them; and their opposites not that I flee, but, as it were, set apart. What do Aristotle and the other pupils of Plato say? That they call all things that are in accordance with nature goods, and those contrary to it evils.

passages.original: Tum Pomponius: At ego, quem vos ut deditum Epicuro insectari soletis, sum multum equidem cum Phaedro, quem unice diligo, ut scitis, in Epicuri hortis, quos modo praeteribamus, sed veteris proverbii admonitu vivorum memini, nec tamen Epicuri licet oblivisci, si cupiam, cuius imaginem non modo in tabulis nostri familiares, sed etiam in poculis et in anulis habent.
passages.english: Then Pomponius said: 'But I, whom you are accustomed to attack as devoted to Epicurus, am often indeed with Phaedrus, whom, as you know, I love above all, in the gardens of Epicurus, which we were just passing; but, reminded by the old proverb, I remember the living. Yet I could not forget Epicurus even if I wished, since our friends have his likeness not only in pictures but even on their cups and their rings.'
passages.notes: The proverb is presumably to be mindful of the living.

passages.original: Et ille, cum erubuisset: Noli, inquit, ex me quaerere, qui in Phalericum etiam descenderim, quo in loco ad fluctum aiunt declamare solitum Demosthenem, ut fremitum assuesceret voce vincere. modo etiam paulum ad dexteram de via declinavi, ut ad Pericli sepulcrum accederem. quamquam id quidem infinitum est in hac urbe; quacumque enim ingredimur, in aliqua historia vestigium ponimus.
passages.english: And he, having blushed, said: 'Do not ask me, who even went down to Phalerum, the place where they say Demosthenes used to declaim against the waves, so as to get used to overcoming the roar with his voice. Just now, too, I turned off the road a little to the right to go up to the tomb of Pericles. Though indeed there is no end to that in this city; wherever we walk, we set our foot on some piece of history.'

passages.original: omnium fere civitatum non Graeciae solum, sed etiam barbariae ab Aristotele mores, instituta, disciplinas, a Theophrasto leges etiam cognovimus. cumque uterque eorum docuisset qualem in re publica principem esse conveniret, pluribus praeterea conscripsisset qui esset optimus rei publicae status, hoc amplius Theophrastus: quae essent in re publica rerum inclinationes et momenta temporum, quibus esset moderandum, utcumque res postularet. vitae autem degendae ratio maxime quidem illis placuit quieta, in contemplatione et cognitione posita rerum, quae quia deorum erat vitae simillima, sapiente visa est dignissima.
passages.english: From Aristotle we have learned the customs, institutions and systems of almost all states, not only of Greece but also of the barbarian world, and from Theophrastus their laws as well. And while each of them had taught what sort of man the leading statesman in a commonwealth ought to be, and had moreover written at length on what the best constitution of a state is, Theophrastus went further: [he set out] what the tendencies of affairs in a state are, and the critical moments of circumstance, which must be managed in whatever way the situation demands. As for the manner of spending one's life, they most of all favoured the quiet one, devoted to the contemplation and knowledge of things, which, because it was most like the life of the gods, seemed most worthy of the wise man.

passages.original: Diodorus, eius auditor, adiungit ad honestatem vacuitatem doloris. hic quoque suus est de summoque bono dissentiens dici vere Peripateticus non potest. antiquorum autem sententiam Antiochus noster mihi videtur persequi diligentissime, quam eandem Aristoteli fuisse et Polemonis docet.
passages.english: Diodorus, his pupil, adds freedom from pain to moral worth. He too is his own man, and, dissenting about the supreme good, cannot truly be called a Peripatetic. But our Antiochus seems to me to follow the view of the ancients most carefully, and he shows that this same view was that of Aristotle and of Polemo.

passages.original: iunctae autem et duplices expositiones summi boni tres omnino fuerunt, nec vero plures, si penitus rerum naturam videas, esse potuerunt. nam aut voluptas adiungi potest ad honestatem, ut Calliphonti Dinomachoque placuit, aut doloris vacuitas, ut Diodoro, aut prima naturae, ut antiquis, quos eosdem Academicos et Peripateticos nominavimus. sed quoniam non possunt omnia simul dici, haec in praesentia nota esse debebunt, voluptatem semovendam esse, quando ad maiora quaedam, ut iam apparebit, nati sumus.
passages.english: But there have been three combined and twofold accounts of the supreme good in all, and indeed there could not have been more, if you look deep into the nature of things. For either pleasure can be joined to moral worth, as Calliphon and Dinomachus held, or freedom from pain, as Diodorus held, or the primary things of nature, as the ancients held, whom we have called both Academics and Peripatetics. But since everything cannot be said at once, these things will have to be taken as known for the present: that pleasure must be set aside, since we are born for certain greater things, as will soon become apparent.

passages.original: necesseque est, si quis sibi ipsi inimicus est, eum quae bona sunt mala putare, bona contra quae mala, et quae appetenda fugere, quae fugienda appetere, quae sine dubio vitae est eversio. neque enim, si non nulli reperiuntur, qui aut laqueos aut alia exitia quaerant aut ut ille apud Terentium, qui decrevit tantisper se minus iniuriae suo nato facere, ut ait ipse, dum fiat miser, inimicus ipse sibi putandus est.
passages.english: And it is necessary, if anyone is an enemy to himself, that he think the things that are good to be bad, and conversely the things that are bad to be good, and that he shun what should be sought and seek what should be shunned, which is without doubt the overturning of life. For even if some people are found who seek out nooses or other means of destruction, or [who act] like that man in Terence who decided that he would do "less wrong to his son," as he himself says, "for as long as he is miserable," [such a person] is not to be thought an enemy to himself.
passages.notes: The Terence reference is to Menedemus in the Heauton Timorumenos ("The Self-Tormentor"). The Latin is compressed and the quotation is partly paraphrased. The phrase "decrevit tantisper se minus iniuriae suo nato facere ... dum fiat miser" is somewhat obscure. It means that he thinks he wrongs his son less so long as he himself is miserable.

passages.original: nec vero dico eorum metum mortis, qui, quia privari se vitae bonis arbitrentur, aut quia quasdam post mortem formidines extimescant, aut si metuant, ne cum dolore moriantur, idcirco mortem fugiant; in parvis enim saepe, qui nihil eorum cogitant, si quando iis ludentes minamur praecipitaturos alicunde, extimescunt. quin etiam ferae, inquit Pacuvius, quíbus abest ad praécavendum intéllegendi astútia, iniecto terrore mortis horrescunt. quis autem de ipso sapiente aliter existimat, quin, etiam cum decreverit esse moriendum, tamen discessu a suis atque ipsa relinquenda luce moveatur?
passages.english: Nor indeed am I speaking of the fear of death of those who flee death because they think they are being deprived of the goods of life, or because they dread certain terrors after death, or if they fear they may die in pain; for small children, who think of none of these things, are often terrified if ever we threaten in play to throw them down from somewhere. Indeed even wild beasts, says Pacuvius, "which lack the cunning of understanding to take precautions," shudder when the terror of death is cast upon them. And who thinks otherwise about the wise man himself than that, even when he has decided he must die, he is nonetheless moved by parting from his own people and by having to leave the light itself?

passages.original: maxime autem in hoc quidem genere vis est perspicua naturae, cum et mendicitatem multi perpetiantur, ut vivant, et angantur adpropinquatione mortis confecti homines senectute et ea perferant, quae Philoctetam videmus in fabulis. qui cum cruciaretur non ferendis doloribus, propagabat tamen vitam aucupio, sagittarum ictu configebat tardus celeres, stans volantis, ut apud Accium est, pennarumque contextu corpori tegumenta faciebat.
passages.english: But the force of nature is most evident in this kind of matter, since many endure beggary in order to live, and men worn out by old age are distressed at the approach of death and endure what we see Philoctetes [endure] in the plays. Though he was tortured by unbearable pains, he still prolonged his life by fowling; "slow, he pierced the swift, standing, the flying" with the stroke of his arrows, as it is in Accius, and from woven feathers he made coverings for his body.

passages.original: neque enim vocum suavitate videntur aut novitate quadam et varietate cantandi revocare eos solitae, qui praetervehebantur, sed quia multa se scire profitebantur, ut homines ad earum saxa discendi cupiditate adhaerescerent. ita enim invitant Ulixem—nam verti, ut quaedam Homeri, sic istum ipsum locum—: O decus Argolicum, quin puppim flectis, Ulixes,Auribus ut nostros possis agnoscere cantus!Nam nemo haec umquam est transvectus caerula cursu,Quin prius adstiterit vocum dulcedine captus,Post variis avido satiatus pectore musis Doctior ad patrias lapsus pervenerit oras.Nos grave certamen belli clademque tenemus,Graecia quam Troiae divino numine vexit,Omniaque e latis rerum vestigia terris.
passages.english:
For it does not seem that they were accustomed to call back those who sailed past by the sweetness of their voices or by some novelty and variety of singing, but because they professed to know many things, so that men clung to their rocks out of desire for learning. For this is how they invite Ulysses (for I have translated this very passage, as [I have] certain [others] of Homer):
O glory of the Argives, why not turn your ship, Ulysses,
so that you may hear our songs with your ears!
For no one has ever sailed across these blue waters on his course
without first standing still, captured by the sweetness of our voices,
and afterwards, his eager heart filled with varied muses,
has glided on, more learned, and reached his native shores.
We know the grievous contest and disaster of war
which Greece brought upon Troy by divine will,
and all the traces of things across the wide lands.
passages.notes: The subject of the first sentence is the Sirens, from the preceding context. In the last line, "tenemus" ("we know") governs "vestigia" as well.

passages.original: quem enim ardorem studii censetis fuisse in Archimede, qui dum in pulvere quaedam describit attentius, ne patriam quidem captam esse senserit? quantum Aristoxeni ingenium consumptum videmus in musicis? quo studio Aristophanem putamus aetatem in litteris duxisse? quid de Pythagora? quid de Platone aut de Democrito loquar?
passages.english: For what ardour of study do you think there was in Archimedes, who, while he was drawing certain figures in the dust rather intently, did not even notice that his native city had been captured? How much of Aristoxenus' talent do we see spent on music? With what zeal do we think Aristophanes passed his life in literature? What [shall I say] of Pythagoras? What shall I say of Plato or of Democritus?
passages.notes: Aristophanes here is probably Aristophanes of Byzantium, the grammarian, not the comic poet.

passages.original: in primo enim ortu inest teneritas ac mollitia quaedam, ut nec res videre optimas nec agere possint. virtutis enim beataeque vitae, quae duo maxime expetenda sunt, serius lumen apparet, multo etiam serius, ut plane qualia sint intellegantur. praeclare enim Plato: Beatum, cui etiam in senectute contigerit, ut sapientiam verasque opiniones assequi possit! Quare, quoniam de primis naturae commodis satis dictum est, nunc de maioribus consequentibusque videamus.
passages.english: For at the very beginning [of life] there is a certain tenderness and softness, so that [the young] can neither see the best things nor do them. For the light of virtue and of the happy life, the two things most to be sought, appears later, and much later still [comes the ability] to understand plainly what they are like. For Plato [said] splendidly: "Happy is he to whom it has fallen, even in old age, to be able to attain wisdom and true opinions!" Therefore, since enough has been said about the primary advantages of nature, let us now look at the greater things that follow from them.

passages.original: dixerit hoc idem Epicurus, semper beatum esse sapientem—quod quidem solet ebullire non numquam—, quem quidem, cum summis doloribus conficiatur, ait dicturum: Quam suave est! quam nihil curo!; non pugnem cum homine, cur tantum habeat in natura boni;
passages.english: Suppose Epicurus says this same thing, that the wise man is always happy (which indeed he is accustomed to blurt out now and then), the wise man who, he says, when he is being worn out by the greatest pains, will say, "How pleasant this is! How little I care!" I would not fight with the man over why he finds so much good in nature;
passages.notes: "Ebullire" literally means "to bubble up." Here it is pejorative: "to blurt out" or "to boast."

passages.original: Theophrasti igitur, inquit, tibi liber ille placet de beata vita?
passages.english: "So," he said, "you like that book of Theophrastus on the happy life?"

passages.original: Audi igitur, inquit, Luci; tecum enim mihi instituenda oratio est. Omnis auctoritas philosophiae, ut ait Theophrastus, consistit in beata vita comparanda; beate enim vivendi cupiditate incensi omnes sumus. hoc mihi cum tuo fratre convenit.
passages.english: "Listen, then, Lucius," he said, "for it is with you that I must begin my discourse. The whole authority of philosophy, as Theophrastus says, consists in procuring the happy life, for we are all inflamed with the desire to live happily. On this I am in agreement with your brother."

passages.original: nisi enim id faceret, cur Plato Aegyptum peragravit, ut a sacerdotibus barbaris numeros et caelestia acciperet? cur post Tarentum ad Archytam? cur ad reliquos Pythagoreos, Echecratem, Timaeum, Arionem, Locros, ut, cum Socratem expressisset, adiungeret Pythagoreorum disciplinam eaque, quae Socrates repudiabat, addisceret? cur ipse Pythagoras et Aegyptum lustravit et Persarum magos adiit? cur tantas regiones barbarorum pedibus obiit, tot maria transmisit?
passages.english: For if he did not do this, why did Plato travel through Egypt, to learn arithmetic and astronomy from barbarian priests? Why [go] afterwards to Archytas at Tarentum? Why to the other Pythagoreans, Echecrates, Timaeus, Arion, at Locri, so that, having portrayed Socrates, he might join to it the teaching of the Pythagoreans and learn besides those things which Socrates rejected? Why did Pythagoras himself both travel through Egypt and visit the magi of the Persians? Why did he go on foot through such great regions of barbarians, and cross so many seas?
passages.notes: 'numeros et caelestia' is literally 'numbers and heavenly things', i.e. mathematics and astronomy. 'Locros' may be taken as the Locrians (Timaeus was of Locri); rendered as 'at Locri'. 'Arionem' is the transmitted reading; some editors emend the name (e.g. to Acrion).

passages.original: semper enim ex eo, quod maximas partes continet latissimeque funditur, tota res appellatur. dicimus aliquem hilare vivere; ergo, si semel tristior effectus est, hilara vita amissa est? at hoc in eo M. Crasso, quem semel ait in vita risisse Lucilius, non contigit, ut ea re minus ἀγέλαστος, ut ait idem, vocaretur. Polycratem Samium felicem appellabant. nihil acciderat ei, quod nollet, nisi quod anulum, quo delectabatur, in mari abiecerat. ergo infelix una molestia, felix rursus, cum is ipse anulus in praecordiis piscis inventus est?
passages.english: For a whole thing is always named from that which contains its greatest parts and extends most widely. We say that someone lives cheerfully; so, if he has once been made rather sad, has his cheerful life been lost? Yet this did not happen in the case of that Marcus Crassus who, Lucilius says, laughed once in his life: that he should on that account be any less called *agelastos* ["the man who never laughs"], as the same [Lucilius] says. They called Polycrates of Samos fortunate. Nothing had happened to him that he did not want, except that he had thrown into the sea a ring in which he took delight. So was he unfortunate because of one annoyance, and fortunate again when that very ring was found in the belly of a fish?
passages.notes: 'ἀγέλαστος' is Greek in the original. 'praecordia' properly the entrails/midriff; rendered 'belly'.
